Bodyweight strength training has a way of developing your lower chest over your upper chest. I had sad droopy pecs for years before I started being careful about it and focusing more on the upper chest. Maybe people who focus purely on strength couldn't give less of a shit, but if you're like me and you care about looks, you probably want teardrop shaped quads, not pecs. But why is it like this? Let's take a look at some common bodyweight exercises and what weight exercises they resemble to find out.

Pushups- the angle is similar to a slightly declined bench press. Not a huge difference, but it's there.

Dips- dips' angle looks a lot like decline bench, assuming you lean forward a lot, as most people do. [Decline bench is known as a lower pec exercise, for those not familiar.] If you do a lot of dips as one of your main chest exercises, your lower pecs will almost certainly be highly developed, which isn't necessarily a bad thing for your aesthetics, as long as your upper chest is developed to match.

Handstand pushups- huh, handstand pushups don't work the chest? That's right, they don't, at least, not the way most people do them. By kicking up against a wall with your back against it, you are forced to keep your body perfectly straight, making the movement look like a very strict military barbell press. This is great for your shoulders and triceps, but not at all great for your upper chest, as it keeps it completely out of a movement that it would naturally be involved in [pressing overhead].

So what can we do to involve this region more in your bodyweight strength training? Consider the following:

Do feet-elevated pushups. If you're like me in the past, you probably consider this a cheap beginner exercise progression, to be forgotten about once you're at even an intermediate level. But what really needs to be thrown out is that mindset, if you want great upper chest development that is. By elevating your feet a significant amount [at least a foot, and up to four feet. No putting your feet on dumbbells and calling it good, that won't work.] you're turning the slightly decline banch-looking pushup into a more upper chest friendly incline bench-resembling exercise.

Do these for high reps if you need to, for teh pumps, and really focus on engaging your upper chest. Keep the movement slow, you're doing this for gains, not explosive strength. Four seconds up and down with no pause or lockout inbetween would be good. If they get way too easy and you get above 25 reps like this, try leaning forward slightly and turning them into semi planche pushups. This shouldn't hurt the upper chest engagement any.

Handstand pushups- simple, do them stomach to wall, or freestanding in an arched handstand. This will allow you to lean forward and engage your upper chest in the movement. Look, I'm not saying do them like this all the time, your standard back-to-wall handstand pushups are still the better shoulder and triceps builder. But if you're concerned with your upper chest, you'd be well advised to do them like this at least some of the time.

Dips- Dips aren't a bad exercise, not at all. They're great for the lower chest. But if your lower chest is already overdeveloped, it wouldn't hurt you any to cut them out. It won't go anywhere, I promise. If your entire chest is underdeveloped, you poor sap, by all means do dips, but balance them out with a more upper-chest focused exercise like feet-elevated pushups [I'm calling them that and not decline pushups just to avoid confusion. Decline pushups = incline bench, they're like a mirror, see?].

If you just love dipping for some reason, and want to keep them in your program, an easy solution would be to stay upright in your dips, thus keeping it a mostly triceps and shoulders exercise. It's not necessary to do these at all though.

Finally, very important here, practice flexing your upper chest in the mirror, and use proactive tension to focus on it during the exercises. Do all the feet-elevated pushups and leaned-forward stomach to wall HSPUs you want, your upper chest will not grow if you can't engage it.

If you're struggling with this, well, I'm not sure I [or anyone else] can tell you how to flex your upper chest. It's something you've just gotta practice and work on yourself. I do have one tip though: rounding your shoulders and leaning forward a bit makes it easier. Once you get it engaged, pull your shoulders back and stand up straight while keeping it engaged. You don't want to only be able to do it in one position. Eventually you should be able to flex it with shoulders pulled back all the way and standing straight up from the get go.

Thomas Midgley, Jr. the inventor of leaded gasoline and freon. He later died from his own invention.

In 1940, at the age of 51, Midgley contracted poliomyelitis, which left him severely disabled. This led him to devise an elaborate system of strings and pulleys to help others lift him from bed. This system was the eventual cause of his own death when he was entangled in the ropes of this device and died of strangulation at the age of 55.

In keeping with his tragic life story, Midgley's legacy has been scarred by the negative environmental impact of some of his innovations. His work led to the release of large quantities of lead into the atmosphere as a result of the large-scale combustion of leaded gasoline all over the world. High atmospheric lead levels have been linked with serious long-term health problems from childhood, including neurological impairment, and with increased levels of violence and criminality in cities.

Midgley died three decades before the ozone-depleting and greenhouse gas effects of CFCs in the atmosphere became widely known. Bill Bryson remarks that Midgley possessed "an instinct for the regrettable that was almost uncanny." J. R. McNeill, an environmental historian, opines that Midgley "had more impact on the atmosphere than any other single organism in Earth's history."
